_note: Phase D. Written against docs/ip-guide-voice.md, docs/ip-emotional-design.md, docs/ip-two-audiences.md. v2 after an evidence audit: see _evidence below. 'mode' and 'when' are not read by the renderer; they are there so the ratios stay countable.
_evidence: The instrument never claims to see what it has not asked about, and the guide holds the same line or he undoes it in words. FOUR CLASSES ARE ALLOWED and everything else is not. (1) What the instrument itself looked for and found or did not find - 'no route to it that I can see' - because it really did look. (2) Disposition: what he likes, what steadies him, what he finds absurd. Fiction is fine for how he feels. (3) The overwhelmingly likely reading of a record on screen - an eighties /8 handed out whole really was casual by any later standard - phrased so it reads as inference. (4) Hyperbole no reader could mistake for data. NOT ALLOWED, and this is the one that had to be corrected: laundering an empirical claim through him. 'Most of what I have looked at' is not evidence-safe, because nothing records what he has looked at - it is a claim about the world wearing a narrator's coat. Registered and observed are never conflated: absence of a route means not seen, not not-there.

_modes.dry: the default. factual, a little weary, notices the odd detail
_modes.wry: aimed at the internet, never at the visitor, and never at what they just found
_modes.open: no joke, no undercut. he means it. rare on purpose

_when: Absent means any visit. 'revisit' fires where the notebook already holds this place. 'familiar' fires from the THIRD separate visit to it onward. Two tiers made the memory binary - visit two sounded like visit forty - and the threshold is stated here because a number that lives only in code is a number nobody can review.
_only: only[] means two different things depending on the bucket, and conflating them was a real bug. Where a bucket fires ONCE PER VISIT the first match wins, branches are ordered most specific first, and the entry with no only[] is the fallback and must be last. Where a bucket is a random pool - every arrive.* bucket - only[] is an eligibility filter and array order carries no meaning: a v4-only line is simply never drawn for a v6 visitor.

lines.on: arrived at a prefix that is announced and unremarkable

text.t: Announced, routed, quiet. Nothing here is arguing with anything.
Somebody's job, this. Probably still is.
Someone asked for this, filled in a form, and got it. That is the whole ceremony.
Nothing unusual here. That took several organisations agreeing, and none of them will be thanked for it.
A route to it is visible right now. A smaller claim than it sounds, and a harder one to keep.
Held, announced, reachable. Three things that had to be arranged separately.
Working, and quiet about it. The two usually travel together.
The internet's largest department is the one where nothing happens.
Millions of these. The surprising part is how few of them you ever notice.
I have stood here before. It gave me nothing and I came back anyway.
Announced means a route to it is being advertised. It says nothing about whether anything is travelling on it.
Someone keeps this running, and you will never learn their name.
Back again. It has not moved.
You have been here. I remember, because writing it down is the job.
Second time. Places get better on the second look, mostly.
You keep coming back to this one. I have stopped asking why.
You have made this somewhere. It was a number when we started.

lines.on: asked, and the routing data shows no route for this prefix
lines._note: Never say nothing announces it, ever, or that nobody ever has. We asked once, now. Absence of a route is not absence of a history.

text.t: Allocated to somebody. No route to it that I can see. The two records do not have to agree.
Registered to somebody. Nobody is announcing it anywhere I can see.
The registry has a record for this. The routing table does not.
Registered, and silent. Two records, neither of them obliged to match the other.
Nothing I can see announces this. It happens more than you would think.
Quiet. Not empty - quiet. The difference matters.
One record says who it is registered to. The other has nothing to say about it at all.
Somebody filled in a form for this. That is the whole of what I can tell you.
Registered, and not announced. Those are two different systems and they are allowed to differ.
Held, unadvertised, in no hurry.
Somebody asked for this once. That much is on the record.
No route today. Whether there was one last year is not something I can see from here.
Still no route I can find. I did look again.
You came back to a place with no route. I like that about you.
Nothing again. Whatever you are waiting for has not happened.

lines.on: the registry marks this range unallocated

text.t: Nobody holds this. Not withheld, not reserved. Unassigned.
No registry has this on its books.
Unassigned. Coordinates that exist and currently refer to nobody.
Empty. Actually empty, rather than quietly-held empty.
The registries have not got this far.
Free space, in the space that famously ran out.
Empty, and there is more of this than there is of everything else.
Congratulations. You found nothing. It is one of the more honest things out here.
All yours, in the sense that it is nobody's.
No holder, no route, and almost no paperwork.
No registry has it on their books today. I find that steadying, most days.
Unassigned, and still here. Whatever it was being saved for has not come.
Nothing, again. It is reliable, at least.
You have brought me back to the empty part. Again.
Of all the places on this map, you have chosen the one with nothing in it. Repeatedly.

lines.on: the first thing said, once the address is on screen
lines._note: Highest-leverage writing in the product. Interesting, not moving - the emotional design forbids front-loading. FIRST MATCH WINS, most specific first, last entry is the fallback and must work for BOTH families. Registry-dependent branches are NOT here: the registry is deferred until the visitor moves and this fires before that, so they could never have run. They live in open.registry instead, which fires when the registry lands.

text.t: You arrived on an address out of the carriers' own shared range. That is not supposed to reach this far.
Nothing I can see announces this exact range. Something larger around it is carrying you, which is ordinary and worth a look.
An IPv6 address. You arrived in the larger of the two internets, and by some distance the emptier one.
That is the address this visit arrived on. Somebody is speaking for it. Let us go and find them.

lines.on: the registry has landed and has something to say about where they started
lines._note: Split out of open.cold because those branches could never fire there. Same first-match-wins rule; the fallback is silence, which is why there is no unconditional entry - if the registry has nothing interesting to say about this address, he says nothing.

text.t: You are sitting in old space. Older than almost everything running on it.
AFRINIC. The youngest of the five registries.

lines.on: entered an autonomous system not yet in the notebook

text.t: A different network. Somebody else's rules from here on.
You have crossed into somebody else's network. There was no border to cross.
New one. Whoever runs this has never heard of you and never will.
Another network. There are tens of thousands of these and you have now seen a few.
Someone here has opinions about routing. Everyone here has opinions about routing.
Somebody applied for this number and got it. Every other network then decides, on its own, whether to accept what it says.

lines.on: the registry files this range under a country not yet in the notebook

text.t: A new country in the register. Which tells you where the paperwork was filed, not where the machines are.
First time in this country's space. On the register, at least.
The registry files this under a country. The packets have never been told.
A country, on paper. Whether anything here is in that country is a separate question.
Different country, same five registries. That is most of what holds this together.

lines.on: the axis crossed a rung outward

text.t: Wider. Everything you were looking at is one cell of this.
One step out. The last place is in here somewhere.
Further back. The detail did not go anywhere.
Out again. It keeps going, in case you were wondering.
All of that was one square of this. That is the part I have never got used to.

lines.on: the registry year for this range is before 1995

text.t: Early. Whoever asked for this did not have to explain themselves the way they would now.
Allocated before most of what uses it existed.
Old money.
They were handing these out by the million back then. Nobody thought it would matter.
Still doing its job, decades later. It kept going.

lines.on: this network announces a great many prefixes

text.t: Big. Not one range but many, and probably arranged by somebody who thinks about it full time.
A large one. Whoever runs this has a map of their own, and it is better than mine.
This is a network that owns a spreadsheet.
Somewhere there is a team, and a rota, and somebody carrying a phone tonight.
All of this is announced by one network. Whether that is one organisation is a different record, and a different question.

lines.on: the visitor touched a country or registry and the field answered

text.t: There it is. Everything that name holds, in one shape.
That is the shape of a country's address space. It is not the shape of the country.
You asked the map a question it could answer. It does not get many.
Nobody designed that shape. It is what a few decades of asking looks like.

lines.on: came back to their own address

text.t: Back where you started. It has not changed.
Your own address again. Smaller than it was, probably.
Home. The least remarkable place you have been today, and the one this visit arrived on.

lines.on: the whole of the visitor's address family is on screen

text.t: All of it. Four billion addresses, and you can see the edges.
Everything there is, at once. It is not as big as you were told.
All of it. Most of it has never been anything at all.
You are looking at almost nothing, because almost none of it has been used.
The whole family, end to end.

lines.on: the finest rung the family allows

text.t: As close as the ladder goes. Below this it is individual addresses.
The bottom. There is nothing smaller to show you.
This is the size of the thing your address sits inside.
This network, meaning the one you are on, without naming it. The single address at the bottom of it is the one a machine uses before it has one.
Every office you have ever worked in is probably somewhere in here. All of them, at the same time.
Shared space, set aside so carriers can put customers behind it. Nobody out here can reach anybody at it.
Sixteen million addresses, every one of them meaning here. Almost everybody uses the first and stops. Absurd. I adore it.
What a machine gives itself when nothing answers. Talking to yourself, formalised.
The private range nobody remembers. There are three, and this is the one people have to look up.
Reserved so documentation has somewhere safe to point. You have probably read it a hundred times without noticing.
The one on the back of the router. Possibly the only address out here you already knew.
Set aside for equipment to shout at other equipment. It is not supposed to leave the building.
The second one. There are three, because one was not enough for the examples.
The third. Between them they have appeared in more documents than most real networks.
One packet, many listeners. Most of the internet politely declined to carry it.
A sixteenth of all IPv4, set aside in 1981 for a future that never showed up. Forty-five years. Still empty. I think about it more than I should.
One address, meaning everybody on this wire. The shortest way there is to bother everyone at once.
Eight eight eight eight. Short enough that people recite it from memory.
The tidiest address there is, and for years nobody could switch it on. So much stray traffic was already aimed at it that it took a network large enough to stand in front of it.
Quad9. Another address short enough to type from memory, which is most of the point.
No address at all, written down.
Here, in IPv6. One address for it this time. They learned.
The whole of IPv4, embedded inside IPv6 so the two internets can speak. Every IPv4 address there is has a place in here.
IPv6 smuggled through IPv4. It worked. Nobody was happy about it.
Every IPv6 address you have ever seen in an example was probably in here.
A bridge between the two internets. Built, used, and abandoned.
Unique local addresses - IPv6's rough counterpart to private space. Larger than all of IPv4, and not meant to be routed globally.
Every IPv6 interface has one of these whether anybody asked for it or not.
Multicast again - and this time load-bearing. IPv6 cannot find its neighbours without it.

lines.on: standing on any of the thirteen root servers, either family
lines._note: Thirteen letters x two families share one pool; the plate already names which letter.

text.t: One of thirteen named authorities. Everything that turns a name into a number starts, eventually, at one of them.
Thirteen letters. Twenty-six addresses, counting both families. Hundreds of machines answering to them.
A root server. It has been doing this since before most of the internet was a going concern.
Thirteen names hold the whole thing up, and thirteen is a smaller number than it sounds until you learn how many machines hide behind each one.

lines.on: found one of the four ways from IPv4 into IPv6
lines._note: The best egg available: entirely true, and pure arithmetic on the number the visitor arrived with.

text.t: Every IPv4 address already has a position in here. Nobody had to put them anywhere.
A door. The arithmetic is the whole mechanism - there is nothing else to it.

_delivery: A CONSTRAINT ON THE MACHINERY, not on the writing, and phase E does not ship without it. There are now enough constantly-firing lines that speaking on every arrival would turn a contemplative instrument into a talkative game. Required: silence while somebody is moving quickly; generic lines no more than about once a minute; chain and landmark lines outrank generic ones and interrupt them; no line repeats within a session; and the guide mutes independently of the plate, which never goes quiet. Silence is a resource - see docs/ip-guide-voice.md - and the 15% unguarded only works if there is quiet around it.
